warmup.q: close(night) is annotated @Retry(attempts = 3) and calls this.verify(night), which is also @Retry(attempts = 3) and always throws a failure that is worth retrying. The part is intercepted by a subclass proxy, so self-calls are intercepted. How many times does verify's body run before close gives up?
warmup.why: Each attempt of close calls verify through the subclass, and verify's own retry runs its body three times before it throws. close's retry then catches that and tries again, three times in all: 3 x 3 = 9. Nested retries multiply. With a forwarding proxy the inner call would skip interception and run once per close attempt, 3 in all, which is why 3 is the tempting answer.

opening:
The city's booking service runs in another building, and the box office reaches it over the network. Most calls come back in a few milliseconds. Now and then one gets no answer: the call times out, and the customer at the counter waits for nothing. So the theatre wants every booking call timed, and a call that timed out tried again.

Writing a timer and a retry loop into every method works, and buries each line of real work under a dozen lines of plumbing. The stand-in at the stage door from the Class loading track did this job for an actor: it noted every request and tried again when the actor didn't answer. The trap is in what you try again. Retry the wrong call, and one customer ends up holding two seats.

Last time, the container built each part from its constructor. In this lesson, it hands out stand-ins, objects called proxies that take each call first: a JDK proxy for a part with an interface, a Byte Buddy subclass for one without. Then we'll make Kotlin's final classes fail loudly and choose which call to retry. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a booking service that sometimes doesn't answer, and plumbing copied into every method. Now two interceptors hold the plumbing, and the container hands out stand-ins: a JDK proxy for a part with an interface, a costume copy from Byte Buddy for one without. At start-up, it refuses any annotation no proxy could reach.

Now look in your own code for a method with an annotation such as @Transactional, @Retry or @Cacheable. Check two things: can a proxy reach it (is it open and public?), and is it ever called through this?

Next, we'll measure what these stand-ins cost. How many classes does one start load, and how much of that work could the build do instead?

sections.h: An interceptor runs around a call, and proceed() passes it on
sections.html:
Here is what timing and retries look like when a method does them itself:

Java
public String reserve(String seat, long priceCents) {
    long t0 = System.nanoTime();
    try {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try { return remote.reserve(seat, priceCents); }        // the one line of real work
            catch (BookingUnavailableException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; }
        }
    } finally {
        timings.record("reserve", System.nanoTime() - t0);
    }
}
Kotlin
fun reserve(seat: String, priceCents: Long): String {
    val t0 = System.nanoTime()
    try {
        var attempt = 1
        while (true) {
            try { return remote.reserve(seat, priceCents) }        // the one line of real work
            catch (e: BookingUnavailableException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e }
        }
    } finally {
        timings.record("reserve", System.nanoTime() - t0)
    }
}

One line of real work and a dozen lines of plumbing, copied into confirm, cancel and every method the booking service will ever grow. Decorator and Proxy moved that plumbing into a class that wraps the real one, but you still write one wrapper per interface. And the timer and the retry are tangled together, so changing one means reading both.

An interceptor is the plumbing written once, for any method. Think of the stand-in at the stage door with one routine: note the time, pass the request on, note the time again. The container hands each interceptor an Invocation, which carries the method's name, its arguments, and proceed(), which means "pass it on". Here is the lab's timer:

Java
public Object intercept(Invocation inv) {
    long start = clock.getAsLong();
    boolean failed = true;
    try {
        Object result = inv.proceed();         // pass it on
        failed = false;
        return result;
    } finally {
        log.record(inv.getName(), clock.getAsLong() - start, failed);
    }
}
Kotlin
override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? {
    val start = clock.asLong
    var failed = true
    try {
        return inv.proceed().also { failed = false }   // pass it on
    } finally {
        log.record(inv.name, clock.asLong - start, failed)
    }
}

Read it in order. First it notes the start time and assumes the worst. Then it passes the call on and, if nothing was thrown, marks it a success. Finally, whatever happened, it records the name, the time taken and the outcome. The finally is the tricky line: it runs on success and on failure, so a call that throws is timed too.

Several interceptors make a chain, like helpers standing in a row at the door. proceed() hands the call to the next helper, and after the last one it runs the real method. A retry interceptor is a loop that calls proceed() again after a failure it was told to retry. Real frameworks have the same shape: InvocationContext.proceed() in Jakarta, the standard set of Java server libraries, and MethodInvocation.proceed() in Spring are this method under other names.

The order of the chain changes what you measure. With the timer outside the retry, it sees one call that took as long as all the attempts together. With the timer inside, it records every attempt on its own. The demo sends one booking call that fails twice through both orders, with a fake clock that moves 10 ms per read. Its two result lines:

  result hold-C12 after 3 calls, log [Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=false)]
  result hold-C12 after 3 calls, log [Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=true), Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=true), Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=false)]

The lab puts @Timed first, outside, because the customer waited for all of it. The annotations themselves only mark methods. Like @Component in lesson 1, they need @Retention(RUNTIME) so the container can read them with getAnnotation. Now the container has to put the chain in front of the real object, and how it does that depends on whether the part has an interface.

try.title: Swap the order of two interceptors
steps: Read ChainDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The "booking service" fails twice and then answers. A third interceptor prints each time the chain reaches it.
Predict, for each order: how many -> lines, and how many entries in the log?
Run it. Then change RetryInterceptor(3, ...) to RetryInterceptor(2, ...) and predict what the first order prints.

code.title: ChainDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.CallLog; import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor; import workbench.container.l02.Invocation; import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor; import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; /** One booking call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. */ public class ChainDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicLong ticks = new AtomicLong(); LongSupplier clock = () -> ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000); // a fake clock: 10 ms per read Interceptor shout = inv -> { // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() System.out.println(" -> " + inv.getName()); try { return inv.proceed(); } finally { System.out.println(" <- " + inv.getName()); } }; for (String order : List.of("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { CallLog log = new CallLog(); Interceptor timed = new TimedInterceptor(log, clock); Interceptor retry = new RetryInterceptor(3, List.of(IllegalStateException.class)); List<Interceptor> chain = order.startsWith("timed") ? List.of(timed, retry, shout) : List.of(retry, timed, shout); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); System.out.println(order + ":"); Object result = new Invocation("Booking.reserve", new Object[] {"C12"}, chain, () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("booking service timed out"); // fails twice return "hold-C12"; }).proceed(); System.out.println(" result " + result + " after " + calls.get() + " calls, log " + log.calls()); } } }

alt.title: ChainDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.CallLog import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor import workbench.container.l02.Invocation import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.function.LongSupplier // One booking call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. fun main() { val ticks = AtomicLong() val clock = LongSupplier { ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000) } // a fake clock: 10 ms per read val shout = Interceptor { inv -> // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() println(" -> ${inv.name}") try { inv.proceed() } finally { println(" <- ${inv.name}") } } for (order in listOf("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { val log = CallLog() val timed = TimedInterceptor(log, clock) val retry = RetryInterceptor(3, listOf(IllegalStateException::class.java)) val chain = if (order.startsWith("timed")) listOf(timed, retry, shout) else listOf(retry, timed, shout) var calls = 0 println("$order:") val result = Invocation("Booking.reserve", arrayOf("C12"), chain) { if (++calls < 3) throw IllegalStateException("booking service timed out") // fails twice "hold-C12" }.proceed() println(" result $result after $calls calls, log ${log.calls()}") } }

try.expect: Both orders print three ->/<- pairs, because the retry calls proceed() three times. With the timer outside, the log has one entry, failed=false, 10 ms on the fake clock. With the retry outside, it has three: two failed=true, one failed=false. With two attempts, the call throws IllegalStateException: booking service timed out after two pairs, and the one log entry is recorded with failed=true on the way out.

video.title: An interceptor runs around a call and proceed() hands it on: a JDK proxy for a component with interfaces, a Byte Buddy subclass for one without, and retry only the smallest call that is safe to repeat

sections.h: A part with an interface gets a stand-in at the stage door: a JDK proxy
sections.html:
For each component, the container now decides how its interceptors will run. If the component implements an interface, it gets a JDK proxy. Proxy.newProxyInstance writes a class that implements the interfaces and sends every call to one InvocationHandler, as Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy showed: the stand-in at the stage door, with the actor behind it. The container creates the real object first, the target, and the proxy holds it. Spring Framework documents the same rule for its own proxies: if the target implements at least one interface, it uses a JDK proxy. (Spring Boot, its quick-start layer, switches the default to subclasses, as Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors showed.)

That lesson's rules for the handler come back as the four cases you write in the lab, in this order:

  1. equals, hashCode and toString arrive with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. Answer them on the proxy itself, by identity. A handler that sends equals to the target makes proxy.equals(proxy) false, and list.remove(proxy) quietly fails.
  2. A default method, an interface method with a body, goes to InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args). Its body then runs with this being the proxy, so the calls inside it come back through the handler.
  3. Every other method gets an Invocation with that method's chain, ending in method.invoke(target, args).
  4. That last call catches InvocationTargetException and throws its cause, so the caller sees the booking service's own BookingUnavailableException, not a wrapper around it.

The demo puts the container's proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, equals included:

bean class: jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5 implements [BookingClient]
container's handler  p.equals(p)=true  listeners.remove(p)=true  hashCode is identity=true
forward everything   p.equals(p)=false  listeners.remove(p)=false  hashCode is identity=false

The forwarding stand-in asked the actor whether the actor was the stand-in, and the actor said no. Fair enough.

Two consequences follow from "the proxy implements the interfaces", and both surprise people. First, the object you get back isn't a FlakyBooking. It's a $Proxy5 that implements BookingClient. get(BookingClient.class) works, but get(FlakyBooking.class) can't return it, so the lab's container refuses with a message that names the interface to ask for:

FlakyBooking is behind a JDK proxy that implements [BookingClient]; ask for one of those, not for the class

Second, the handler only ever sees the interface's Method, so the annotations must sit on the interface. @Timed on the class's method would never be read, and nothing would say so. The container refuses that case when it starts, rather than skip the timer in silence.

Kotlin's final classes don't matter on this path. FakeBooking in the tests is a plain, final Kotlin class, and that's fine: the JDK needs only the interface. A part without an interface is a different story.

try.title: Ask two proxies whether they equal themselves
steps: Read ProxyIdentityDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It compares the container's proxy with one whose handler forwards every method to the target.
Predict the three booleans on each line.
Run it, and read the last line.

code.title: ProxyIdentityDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.Container; import workbench.container.l02.ContainerException; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** The container's JDK proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, equals included. */ public class ProxyIdentityDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Container c = new Container(List.of(BookingScript.class, FlakyBooking.class)); BookingClient booking = c.get(BookingClient.class); System.out.println("bean class: " + booking.getClass().getName() + " implements " + Arrays.stream(booking.getClass().getInterfaces()).map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); report("container's handler", booking); FlakyBooking target = new FlakyBooking(new BookingScript()); InvocationHandler forwardAll = (proxy, method, a) -> method.invoke(target, a); // equals goes to the target too report("forward everything", (BookingClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( BookingClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {BookingClient.class}, forwardAll)); try { c.get(FlakyBooking.class); } catch (ContainerException e) { System.out.println("get(FlakyBooking.class): " + e.getMessage()); } } static void report(String name, BookingClient p) { List<BookingClient> listeners = new ArrayList<>(List.of(p)); System.out.printf("%-20s p.equals(p)=%s listeners.remove(p)=%s hashCode is identity=%s%n", name, p.equals(p), listeners.remove(p), p.hashCode() == System.identityHashCode(p)); } }

alt.title: ProxyIdentityDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.Container import workbench.container.l02.ContainerException import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // The container's JDK proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, equals included. fun main() { val c = Container(listOf(BookingScript::class.java, FlakyBooking::class.java)) val booking = c.get(BookingClient::class.java) println("bean class: ${booking.javaClass.name} implements ${booking.javaClass.interfaces.map { it.simpleName }}") report("container's handler", booking) val target = FlakyBooking(BookingScript()) val forwardAll = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray())) } // equals too report("forward everything", Proxy.newProxyInstance( BookingClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(BookingClient::class.java), forwardAll) as BookingClient) try { c.get(FlakyBooking::class.java) } catch (e: ContainerException) { println("get(FlakyBooking::class.java): ${e.message}") } } private fun report(name: String, p: BookingClient) { val listeners = mutableListOf(p) println("%-20s p.equals(p)=%s listeners.remove(p)=%s hashCode is identity=%s".format( name, p.equals(p), listeners.remove(p), p.hashCode() == System.identityHashCode(p))) }

try.expect: The bean is jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5 (the number depends on how many proxies the JVM made before, annotation instances included) and implements [BookingClient]. The container's handler gives true true true. Forwarding everything gives false false false: the target was asked whether it equals the proxy, and said no. The last line is the container refusing get(FlakyBooking.class): FlakyBooking is behind a JDK proxy that implements [BookingClient]; ask for one of those, not for the class.

sections.h: A part without an interface gets a costume copy: a Byte Buddy subclass, so final is fatal
sections.html:
ShowCloser closes the box office after the last show of the night. It checks the night's code, files the night in the archive, and returns a short note. It has no interface, so there is no job card for a stand-in to copy. Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors had the answer: the costume department sews a full copy of the costume, a subclass that extends the class and replaces some of its methods. Byte Buddy, a library that writes classes while your program runs, does the sewing.

Byte Buddy's subclass(type) copies the class's public constructors. The container calls the generated ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... constructor with the ShowArchive it resolved, and the original class is never created on its own. There is one object. Each intercepted method becomes an override whose @SuperCall callable, a small object that runs super.close(...), sits at the end of the chain. A retry simply calls it again.

Because the subclass is the object, a self-call, a call from one of the object's methods to another through this, goes through it too. close calls this.verify(night). this is the subclass, so verify's override runs its own chain. The Class loading track called this the understudy who plays the role, as against the lookalike at the door who passes requests to the actor. The figure shows both: the JDK proxy is the lookalike, and the actor's own calls never pass the door. The lab's test closes night N-17 and reads the log: [ShowCloser.verify, ShowCloser.close]. verify comes first because each timer records when its call ends, and verify ends inside close.

A subclass can only intercept what it's allowed to override, and Kotlin makes that a daily problem. A Kotlin class is final unless you write open, and so is each of its members: a role nobody may copy. On a final class, Byte Buddy fails loudly: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. On an open class with a plain fun, it succeeds and simply leaves the method alone. @Timed sits on it and does nothing. That silent case is why the lab's container calls check(component) for every component when it starts. It refuses a final class, or a final or private intercepted method, with a message that says what to change. The demo tries two Kotlin classes with the same @Timed method, and the build opens only the second:

KFinalPrices: class final=true, feeCents final=true
  refused: KFinalPrices is final, so no subclass can intercept it: make it open, or give it an interface
KOpenedPrices: class final=false, feeCents final=false
  wired as KOpenedPrices$ByteBuddy$w7Szn3cT, timed calls [KOpenedPrices.feeCents]

There are three fixes. Write open on the class and on each intercepted method. Or let the all-open compiler plugin do it for classes that carry an annotation you choose; this lab's build opens classes marked @OpenForProxies:

// container/build.gradle.kts
plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") }
allOpen { annotation("workbench.container.l02.demo.OpenForProxies") }

kotlin-spring is the same plugin, preset to open the classes Spring creates. The third fix is an interface, which moves the part to the JDK proxy path, where finality doesn't matter. (Quarkus goes a fourth way: by default it rewrites final classes while the program is built, so that it can subclass them.)

An annotation only works if a proxy can reach the method. Make the container refuse what no proxy can reach.

Each class Byte Buddy writes also gets a class loader of its own, a ByteArrayClassLoader, unless you choose another loading strategy. Lesson 3 counts what that leaves behind.

try.title: Watch a Kotlin class get refused, then opened
steps: Read FinalClassDemo.kt: two identical classes with a @Timed method, one marked @OpenForProxies. The Java twin, FinalClassDemoJava, does the same with a Java final class.
Predict the final= flags on each line, and which class the container refuses. Run it.
From labs/, run javap -p container/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/container/l02/demo/KOpenedPrices.class and compare it with KFinalPrices.class.

code.title: FinalClassDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy import workbench.container.l02.Component import workbench.container.l02.Container import workbench.container.l02.ContainerException import workbench.container.l02.Timed import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Two Kotlin classes with the same @Timed method. The build's all-open plugin opens only the second. @Component class KFinalPrices { @Timed fun feeCents(priceCents: Long) = (priceCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 } @OpenForProxies @Component class KOpenedPrices { @Timed fun feeCents(priceCents: Long) = (priceCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 } fun main() { for (type in listOf(KFinalPrices::class.java, KOpenedPrices::class.java)) { val fee = type.getMethod("feeCents", Long::class.java) println("${type.simpleName}: class final=${Modifier.isFinal(type.modifiers)}, feeCents final=${Modifier.isFinal(fee.modifiers)}") try { val c = Container(listOf(type)) val bean = c.get(type) fee.invoke(bean, 12_000L) println(" wired as ${bean.javaClass.simpleName}, timed calls ${c.callLog().names()}") } catch (e: ContainerException) { println(" refused: ${e.message}") } } try { ByteBuddy().subclass(KFinalPrices::class.java).make() // what you get without the check } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("Byte Buddy on its own: ${e.message}") } }

Java classes are open unless you write final. */ public class FinalClassDemoJava { @Component public static final class FinalPrices { @Timed public long feeCents(long priceCents) { return (priceCents * 29 + 500) / 1000; } } @Component public static class OpenPrices { @Timed public long feeCents(long priceCents) { return (priceCents * 29 + 500) / 1000; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Class<?> type : List.of(FinalPrices.class, OpenPrices.class)) { Method fee = type.getMethod("feeCents", long.class); System.out.printf("%s: class final=%s, feeCents final=%s%n", type.getSimpleName(), Modifier.isFinal(type.getModifiers()), Modifier.isFinal(fee.getModifiers())); try { Container c = new Container(List.of(type)); Object bean = c.get(type); fee.invoke(bean, 12_000L); System.out.println(" wired as " + bean.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", timed calls " + c.callLog().names()); } catch (ContainerException e) { System.out.println(" refused: " + e.getMessage()); } } try { new ByteBuddy().subclass(FinalPrices.class).make(); // what you get without the check } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("Byte Buddy on its own: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

KOpenedPrices has both flags false, is wired as KOpenedPrices$ByteBuddy$... (a random suffix) and logs [KOpenedPrices.feeCents]. The last line is Byte Buddy's own error for the final class. In the Java twin only the class is final (feeCents final=false), because Java methods are open by default. In javap, KFinalPrices is public final class with public final long feeCents(long), while KOpenedPrices has neither final.

aside.title: Could an agent add the timer instead?
aside.html: Yes, and many monitoring tools do. Java agents and instrumentation pictured an agent as the stage manager who slips a note into the prompt book before rehearsal: it rewrites a method's bytecode as the class loads. Because the code itself changes, self-calls, final classes and private methods are all covered. The price is a flag on the command line, -javaagent, or a warning since JDK 21 when an agent attaches to a program that is already running. A container usually prefers proxies, because they need nothing from whoever starts the program.

sections.h: Retry the smallest call that is safe to repeat
sections.html:
A retry interceptor makes three promises. It only retries the failures the annotation lists: a BookingUnavailableException is worth another try, a seat that doesn't exist is not. It counts attempts in total, so attempts = 3 means at most three calls. And when it gives up, the caller gets the original exception, not an UndeclaredThrowableException or an InvocationTargetException wrapped around it.

The hard part is choosing which call to repeat. Selling a ticket takes two calls to the booking service: reserve holds the seat, and confirm turns the hold into a ticket. reserveAndConfirm is a default method that makes both:

Java
default String reserveAndConfirm(String seat, long priceCents) {
    return confirm(reserve(seat, priceCents));
}
Kotlin
fun reserveAndConfirm(seat: String, priceCents: Long): String = confirm(reserve(seat, priceCents))

Say the first confirm times out. A handler that forwards the default method to the target, and retries it as a whole, repeats the reservation too. The demo's booking service keeps a list of every call it saw:

container's proxy:  ticket-hold-C12, booking service saw [reserve, confirm (timed out), confirm]
  timed calls: [BookingClient.reserve, BookingClient.confirm]
retry the shell:    ticket-hold-C12, booking service saw [reserve, confirm (timed out), reserve, confirm]

Both halves print a ticket, and the second also held a second seat: one customer, two seats, and an empty one on the night that nobody else can buy. Through the container, invokeDefault runs the default body on the proxy, so each inner call carries its own @Retry, and the confirmation is retried as a confirmation. That's the rule for default methods from Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and the lab tests it.

Even a single call is only safe to repeat if the other side can spot the repeat. A timeout doesn't tell you the booking service didn't confirm. It tells you that you don't know. So retry confirm only if it carries a booking reference, the same one on every attempt, which the service uses to recognize a repeat and do the work once. The general name for such a reference is an idempotency key. The interceptor can't know whether a call carries one; the person who writes @Retry on the method has to.

Retries also multiply when they nest. With a subclass proxy, a retried close that calls a retried verify runs verify's body up to 3 x 3 = 9 times, as the warm-up asked.

A retry repeats whatever you annotate, harmful or not. Put @Retry on the smallest call that is safe to repeat, and only once along a chain of calls.

Here the stand-in picture breaks. A real stand-in would notice the same customer coming back twice for the same seat. An interceptor notices nothing. It does exactly what the annotation says, as many times as it says.

try.title: Retry the confirmation, not the reservation
steps: Read RetryDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The booking service's first confirmation times out. The first half uses the container's proxy; the second uses a handler that retries every method as a whole.
Predict the list of calls the booking service sees in each half.

code.title: RetryDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.Container; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingUnavailableException; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.List; /** reserveAndConfirm, with one confirmation timing out: what does the booking service see? */ public class RetryDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Container c = new Container(List.of(BookingScript.class, FlakyBooking.class)); BookingScript script = c.get(BookingScript.class); script.confirmFailures.set(1); String result = c.get(BookingClient.class).reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000); System.out.println("container's proxy: " + result + ", booking service saw " + script.seen); System.out.println(" timed calls: " + c.callLog().names()); BookingScript naiveScript = new BookingScript(); naiveScript.confirmFailures.set(1); FlakyBooking target = new FlakyBooking(naiveScript); InvocationHandler retryEverything = (proxy, method, a) -> { // retries any method, default ones too for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, a); // the default body runs on the target } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { if (attempt == 3 || !(e.getCause() instanceof BookingUnavailableException)) throw e.getCause(); } } }; BookingClient naive = (BookingClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( BookingClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {BookingClient.class}, retryEverything); System.out.println("retry the shell: " + naive.reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000) + ", booking service saw " + naiveScript.seen); } }

alt.title: RetryDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.Container import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingUnavailableException import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Method import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // reserveAndConfirm, with one confirmation timing out: what does the booking service see? fun main() { val c = Container(listOf(BookingScript::class.java, FlakyBooking::class.java)) val script = c.get(BookingScript::class.java) script.confirmFailures.set(1) val result = c.get(BookingClient::class.java).reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000) println("container's proxy: $result, booking service saw ${script.seen}") println(" timed calls: ${c.callLog().names()}") val naiveScript = BookingScript().apply { confirmFailures.set(1) } val target = FlakyBooking(naiveScript) val retryEverything = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> callWithRetry(target, method, a) } // any method, defaults too val naive = Proxy.newProxyInstance(BookingClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(BookingClient::class.java), retryEverything) as BookingClient println("retry the shell: ${naive.reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000)}, booking service saw ${naiveScript.seen}") } private fun callWithRetry(target: Any, method: Method, a: Array<Any?>?, attempt: Int = 1): Any? = try { method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray())) // the default body runs on the target } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { if (attempt == 3 || e.cause !is BookingUnavailableException) throw e.cause!! callWithRetry(target, method, a, attempt + 1) }

try.expect: Both halves return ticket-hold-C12. Through the container the booking service sees [reserve, confirm (timed out), confirm], and the timed calls are reserve and confirm: the default method itself is not timed. The naive handler gives [reserve, confirm (timed out), reserve, confirm]: one customer, two seats held.

compare.title: A part a subclass can intercept, in Java and in Kotlin

java.title: ShowCloser.java
java.html: @Component public class ShowCloser { // open unless you write final private final ShowArchive archive; public ShowCloser(ShowArchive archive) { this.archive = archive; } @Timed public String close(String night) { // overridable verify(night); // self-call: intercepted in a subclass archive.file(night); return "closed " + night; } @Timed public void verify(String night) { /* ... */ } public final String hall() { return "Main hall"; } // final on purpose: not intercepted }

kotlin.title: ShowCloser.kt
kotlin.html: @Component open class ShowCloser(private val archive: ShowArchive) { // final without open @Timed open fun close(night: String): String { // final without open verify(night) // self-call: intercepted in a subclass archive.file(night) return "closed $night" } @Timed open fun verify(night: String) { /* ... */ } fun hall(): String = "Main hall" // final by default: not intercepted }

compare.note: The two classes compile to the same shape only after you add open in Kotlin. Java's default is overridable, so final is the exception you write; Kotlin's default is final, so open is. That single difference decides whether a subclass proxy can work, and on an open class with a plain fun it fails silently. The all-open plugin flips Kotlin's default for classes with an annotation you choose. Nothing differs for JDK proxies: both languages compile interfaces to ordinary JVM interfaces, and Kotlin interface functions with a body become JVM default methods that invokeDefault can run.

steps.say: The theatre wants every cancellation written down with its arguments, so that a customer's complaint can be checked later. Start with the marker. It needs RUNTIME retention and targets methods, like @Timed.
steps.code: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) public @interface Recorded { }

alt.html: @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) annotation class Recorded

steps.say: Write the interceptor. It writes the call down before it passes it on, so an attempt that throws is on the record too. It doesn't catch anything: failures are the retry's business, or the caller's.
steps.code: public final class RecordInterceptor implements Interceptor { private final List<String> record; public RecordInterceptor(List<String> record) { this.record = record; } @Override public Object intercept(Invocation inv) { record.add(inv.getName() + Arrays.toString(inv.getArgs())); // 1. write it down first return inv.proceed(); // 2. then pass it on } }

alt.html: class RecordInterceptor(private val record: MutableList<String>) : Interceptor { override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? { record += inv.name + inv.args.contentToString() // 1. write it down first return inv.proceed() // 2. then pass it on } }

steps.say: Decide where it goes in the chain. Outside @Retry, it writes one entry per cancellation the customer asked for. Inside, it writes every attempt. The theatre asked for every request sent to the booking service, so it goes inside: after the timer and the retry.
steps.code: List<Interceptor> chainFor(Method m) { List<Interceptor> chain = new ArrayList<>(); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class)) chain.add(new TimedInterceptor(log, clock)); Retry r = m.getAnnotation(Retry.class); if (r != null) chain.add(new RetryInterceptor(r.attempts(), List.of(r.on()))); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Recorded.class)) chain.add(new RecordInterceptor(record)); // 3. innermost return chain; }

alt.html: fun chainFor(m: Method): List<Interceptor> = buildList { if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed::class.java)) add(TimedInterceptor(log, clock)) m.getAnnotation(Retry::class.java)?.let { add(RetryInterceptor(it.attempts, it.on.map { k -> k.java })) } if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Recorded::class.java)) add(RecordInterceptor(record)) // 3. innermost }

steps.say: Teach the container that @Recorded counts as intercepted, in isIntercepted, so check refuses a final recorded method too. Then test through the container: a cancellation that times out once leaves two entries with the same booking reference. If it leaves one, the interceptor sits outside the retry; if it leaves none, the method was never overridden.

lab.title: Write the retry, the proxy handler and the start-up check
steps: Run the tests once. Eleven of twelve fail. The Java files in src/main/java/.../l02 are lesson 1's solution; Container now hands every component to Interception. The Kotlin files are yours. The fixtures are in src/test/kotlin/.../l02/Fixtures.kt: a scripted fake booking service and a few classes the container must refuse.
Write RetryInterceptor.intercept: a loop around inv.proceed() that rethrows on the last attempt, or on an exception that isn't an instance of anything in retryOn.
Write InterceptingHandler.invoke with the four cases from its KDoc, in order. args is null for methods without parameters.
Write the class half of Interception.check: refuse a final class that has intercepted methods, then an intercepted method that is private or final, with the messages from the comment.
Run the tests. Most now fail with your own message: ShowCloser is final, so no subclass can intercept it.... Open ShowCloser and its two @Timed methods. Leave hall() final. Run until all twelve pass.
hints: In Kotlin, Any::class.java is java.lang.Object. That is what method.declaringClass is for equals, hashCode and toString.
InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *a) needs a non-null array: use args ?: emptyArray() once at the top.
If gives up after the last attempt sees UndeclaredThrowableException, your target call threw the InvocationTargetException itself. Throw e.cause!!.
If the self-call test logs only close, verify is still final: open on the class doesn't open its members.
lab.done: All twelve tests in InterceptionTest pass, and hall() is still final.

drill.title: The four-case handler from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write an InvocationHandler for a target and a Map<Method, List<Interceptor>> that answers Object methods by identity, runs default methods with invokeDefault, runs every other method through its chain, and unwraps InvocationTargetException. Then compare. Which case did you write last, and does the order matter?

answer.html: class InterceptingHandler( private val target: Any, private val chains: Map<Method, List<Interceptor>>, ) : InvocationHandler { override fun invoke(proxy: Any, method: Method, args: Array<Any?>?): Any? { val a = args ?: emptyArray() if (method.declaringClass == Any::class.java) return when (method.name) { // 1. identity "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Proxy[$target]" } if (method.isDefault) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *a) // 2. this = proxy return Invocation("${method.declaringClass.simpleName}.${method.name}", a, chains[method].orEmpty()) { try { method.invoke(target, *a) } // 3. the chain, then the target catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } // 4. unwrap }.proceed() } }

alt.html: final class InterceptingHandler implements InvocationHandler { private final Object target; private final Map<Method, List<Interceptor>> chains; InterceptingHandler(Object target, Map<Method, List<Interceptor>> chains) { this.target = target; this.chains = chains; } @Override public Object invoke(Object proxy, Method method, Object[] args) throws Throwable { Object[] a = args == null ? new Object[0] : args; if (method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. identity return switch (method.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == a[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Proxy[" + target + "]"; }; } if (method.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, a); // 2. this = proxy String name = method.getDeclaringClass().getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName(); return new Invocation(name, a, chains.getOrDefault(method, List.of()), () -> { try { return method.invoke(target, a); } // 3. the chain, then the target catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw sneaky(e.getCause()); } // 4. unwrap }).proceed(); } // Callable.call() may throw Exception but not Throwable: rethrow the cause unchanged @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") private static <E extends Throwable> E sneaky(Throwable t) throws E { throw (E) t; } }

recap: An interceptor runs around a call and calls proceed() to pass it on; a chain of them ends in the real method. A retry calls proceed() again. @Timed outside @Retry times what the customer waited for.

A part with interfaces gets a JDK proxy around a separate target. The handler answers equals, hashCode and toString by identity, runs default methods with invokeDefault, runs the chain, and unwraps InvocationTargetException.
A JDK proxy is not an instance of the class and sees only the interface's methods: ask for the interface, and put the annotations there.

A part without interfaces gets a Byte Buddy subclass, built with its real constructor arguments. It is the object itself, so self-calls are intercepted, but it can't extend a final class or override a final or private method. Kotlin is final by default: open the class and the methods, use all-open, or add an interface.
Retry only listed failures, rethrow the original, retry the inner calls of a default method one by one, and repeat only calls that carry a booking reference. Nested retries multiply.
Where today's container stops: every stand-in is made while the program starts, by reflection and by Byte Buddy, and nobody has counted what that costs. Lesson 3 measures it.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the container uses two kinds of proxy instead of always generating a subclass with Byte Buddy. Explain what each kind gives up, and how the container decides.
explain.answer: A JDK proxy needs only an interface. It works on final Kotlin classes and needs no bytecode library, but it's a separate object in front of the target: the part isn't an instance of the class, the annotations must be on the interface, and self-calls inside the target skip the interceptors. A subclass is the object itself, so self-calls are intercepted and the object is an instance of the class, but it can only intercept what it can override: no final classes, no final or private methods, which in Kotlin means writing open or using all-open. The container uses the JDK proxy whenever the component implements an interface, because that path has fewer ways to fail silently, and a subclass only when there is no interface. In both cases it checks at start-up and refuses what it can't intercept.

deeper.html:
Jakarta Interceptors, the standard behind CDI and Quarkus, has the same pieces under other names. An interceptor binding is an annotation like @Timed that is itself annotated @InterceptorBinding. The interceptor is a class with an @AroundInvoke method that takes an InvocationContext and calls ctx.proceed(). The order of the chain comes from @Priority on each interceptor class, with lower numbers running first. Spring AOP's equivalent is an AOP Alliance MethodInterceptor, whose invoke(MethodInvocation) also ends in proceed(), ordered by @Order or the Ordered interface.

Annotations and proxies have a quieter interaction too. Java annotations are not inherited from interfaces: @Timed on BookingClient.reserve is not visible through FakeBooking.class.getMethod("reserve", ...). A JDK proxy hands the handler the interface's Method, so the lab's container sees it. A subclass proxy looks at the class's methods, so an annotation that lives only on an interface method would not be found there. Spring papers over this with its own annotation search, which walks interfaces and superclasses. The lab refuses the doubtful case instead: annotations on the class of an interface-proxied component are an error.

Byte Buddy can also load a generated class without a new class loader. ClassLoadingStrategy.UsingLookup, with a MethodHandles.Lookup from the part's package, defines the subclass in the same loader and package as its superclass. That lets it override package-private methods and avoids one loader per class. The lab uses the default, the simplest strategy, and lesson 3's histogram shows what it leaves behind.
